deep.reconstruction:
This page continues a preliminary section on decreasing rearrangements. It is groundwork for §2 'Fonctions de Weyl' on the next page, which treats symmetric, convex, lower-semicontinuous functionals on functions up to equimeasurability.

Setting: (M, μ) is a measure space of finite total mass |M| < +∞, and f is a real (not necessarily positive) measurable function. Earlier versions of the hypotheses are struck out: that φ_f be finite-valued, or bounded, or a condition on |f^{-1}(f(0))|. Under finiteness of |M|, the page states that there is a unique decreasing function φ_f on ]0, |M|[ equimeasurable with f, i.e. μ{f > a} = λ{φ_f > a} for all a. This is the decreasing rearrangement f*, now extended from positive to real-valued functions; finite measure is needed so that negative values can be placed at the right end of the interval.

Proposition 2 ('classical'): for real measurable f, g on M with |M| < ∞, fg is integrable if and only if φ_f φ_g is, and then
(17) ∫_M fg dμ ≤ ∫_0^{|M|} φ_f(s) φ_g(s) ds.
This is the Hardy–Littlewood rearrangement inequality.

Purpose: together with the previous page, this sets up machinery for symmetric functionals of the spectrum. The previous page had Δ(f) = exp ∫ log|f| dμ, a commutative Fuglede–Kadison-type determinant, and partial versions Δ_{1+f}(t) built from φ_f. That machinery feeds the 'Weyl functions' of the next page. Those are the function-space analogue of symmetric gauge functions and rearrangement-invariant norms, used for Weyl-type eigenvalue inequalities. The likely context is Grothendieck's 1953–56 work on Fredholm theory and nuclear operators.
errors: The 'iff' integrability claim in Proposition 2 is false as stated. Necessity fails even for positive functions. Example: take f, g ≥ 0 with disjoint supports, each behaving like (distance to a point)^{-1/2}. Then fg = 0 is integrable, but φ_f φ_g ~ 1/s is not integrable at 0.

For signed functions, sufficiency also fails. Example on [0,1]: f = x^{-a} on ]0,1/2[ and 0 elsewhere; g = -x^{-a} on ]0,1/2[ and bounded positive on [1/2,1[, with 1/2 ≤ a < 1. Then fg = -x^{-2a} is not integrable. But φ_f φ_g is integrable: near 0 it is φ_f times a bounded φ_g, and near |M| it is 0 times something large.

Correct statement: for f, g ≥ 0, integrability of φ_f φ_g implies integrability of fg, and inequality (17) holds. For signed functions one needs e.g. φ_f φ_g ∈ L^1 together with suitable control of the positive and negative parts. The transcription's 'il faut [?]' may reflect his own hesitation.
Existence and uniqueness of φ_f should be understood up to values at the countably many discontinuity points (choice of left- or right-continuity). This is minor.

ideas.what: Decreasing rearrangement of a real-valued (signed) measurable function on a finite measure space, as the unique decreasing equimeasurable function on ]0,|M|[
ideas.where_published: Possibly background to 'La théorie de Fredholm' (Bull. SMF 1956) / Produits tensoriels topologiques (1955); unsure

deep.surprise_reason: The page states a classical result (the Hardy–Littlewood rearrangement inequality) that Grothendieck himself calls 'classique', with a slightly overstated integrability equivalence. Its interest lies only as groundwork for the 'fonctions de Weyl' and determinant material on the adjacent pages.
